title: Magic has no power over those who pray
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα ὡσπερεὶ ἐπιλαθόμενος οτι κατὰ Χριστιανῶν αὐτῷ πρόκειται γράφειν φησὶ Διονύσιόν τινα μουσικὸν Αἰγύπτιον συγγενόμενον αὐτῷ εἰρηκέναι περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὴν μαγείαν ὅτι πρὸς ἀπαιδεύτους μὲν αὐτὴ δύναται καὶ πρὸς διαφθαρέντας τὰ ἤθη, πρὸς δὲ τοὺς φιλοσοφήσαντας οὐδὲν οἵα τε ἐστὶν ἐνεργεῖν, ἅτε τῆς ὑγιεινῆς διαίτης προνοησαμένους. εἰ μὲν οὖν προέκειτο περὶ μαγείας νῦν ἡμῖν διαλαβεῖν, κἂν προσεθήκαμεν [ἐν] οἷς ἀνωτέρω περὶ αὐτῆς εἰρήκαμεν εἰς τοῦτο ὀλίγα· ἐπεὶ δὲ τὰ ἐπικαιρότερα χρὴ λέγειν πρὸς τὸ Κέλσου σύγγραμμα, περὶ μαγείας φαμὲν ὅτι ὁ βουλόμενος ἐξετάσαι, πότερόν ποτε καὶ φιλόσοφοι ἁλωτοί εἰσιν αὐτῇ ἢ μὴ, ἀναγνώτω τὰ γεγραμμένα Μοιραγένει τῶν Ἀπολλωνίου τοῦ Τυανέως μάγου καὶ φιλοσόφου ἀπομνημονευμάτων· ἐν οἷς ὁ μὴ Χριστιανὸς ἀλλὰ φιλόσοφος ἔφησεν ἁλῶναι ὑπὸ τῆς ἐν Ἀπολλωνίῳ μαγείας οὐκ ἀγεννεῖς τινας φιλοσόφους ὡς πρὸς γόητα αὐτὸν εἰσελθόντας· ἐν οἷς οἶμαι καὶ περὶ Εὐφράτου (τοῦ) πάνυ διηγήσατο καί τινος Ἐπικουρείου. διαβεβαιούμεθα δὲ ἡμεῖς καὶ τῇ πείρᾳ παραλαβόντες ὅτι οἱ κατὰ χριστιανισμὸν διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεραπεύοντες θεὸν καὶ βιοῦντες κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον αὐτοῦ ταῖς προσταχθείσαις τε εὐχαῖς συνεχέστερον καὶ δεόντως νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας χρώμενοι οὔτε μαγείᾳ οὔτε δαιμονίοις εἰσὶν ἁλωτοί. ἀληθῶς γὰρ „παρεμβαλεῖ ἄγγελος κυρίου κύκλῳ τῶν φοβουμένων αὐτὸν καὶ ῥύσεται αὐτοὺς“ ἀπὸ παντὸς κακοῦ· καὶ „οἱ ἄγγελοι“ τῶν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ μικρῶν καὶ τεταγμένοι εἰς τὸ προΐστασθαι αὐτῶν „διὰ παντὸς“ λέγονται βλέπειν „τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖς πατρὸς,“ ὅ τι ποτ᾿ ἐστὶ τὸ πρόσωπον καὶ ὅ τι ποτ᾿ ἐστὶ τὸ βλέπειν.
pass_a_gloss: After these, as if having forgotten (ἐπιλανθάνομαι) that it is set before him (πρόκειται) to write against Christians, he says that a certain Dionysius, an Egyptian musician (μουσικός), having associated (συγγίγνομαι) with him, said about the things of magic (μαγεία) that toward the uneducated (ἀπαίδευτοι) it has power (δύναμαι) and toward those corrupted (διαφθείρω) in character (ἤθη), but toward those who have philosophized (φιλοσοφέω) it is able to effect (ἐνεργέω) nothing, since they have provided for (προνοέω) a healthy regimen (ὑγιεινὴ δίαιτα). If then it were set before us now to treat (διαλαμβάνω) of magic, we would have added (προστίθημι) a few things on this to what we said above about it; but since one must say the more pertinent (ἐπικαιρότερα) things against Celsus's treatise (σύγγραμμα), about magic we say that the one wishing to examine whether perhaps even philosophers are capturable (ἁλωτοί) by it or not, let him read (ἀναγιγνώσκω) the things written by Moeragenes of the memoirs (ἀπομνημονεύματα) of Apollonius of Tyana, magician (μάγος) and philosopher; in which the not-Christian but philosopher said that not ignoble (ἀγεννεῖς) certain philosophers were captured (ἁλίσκομαι) by the magic in Apollonius, having gone in to him as to a sorcerer (γόης); in which I think he narrated also about the very famous (πάνυ) Euphrates and a certain Epicurean. But we affirm (διαβεβαιόομαι), having received (παραλαμβάνω) it also by trial (πεῖρα), that those who according to Christianity (χριστιανισμός) through Jesus serve (θεραπεύω) the God over all (ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός) and live (βιόω) according to his gospel (εὐαγγέλιον) and use the commanded (προστάσσω) prayers (εὐχαί) more continuously (συνεχέστερον) and duly (δεόντως) night and day are capturable neither by magic nor by demons (δαιμόνια). For truly the angel of the Lord will encamp (παρεμβάλλω) around those fearing him and will rescue (ῥύομαι) them from every evil; and the angels of the little ones (μικροί) in the Church, also appointed (τάσσω) to preside over (προΐσταμαι) them, are said always (διὰ παντός) to see (βλέπω) the face (πρόσωπον) of the Father in the heavens, whatever the face is and whatever the seeing is.
pass_b_english: After this, as if he had forgotten that his task is to write against Christians, he says that a certain Dionysius, an Egyptian musician, who had spent time with him, said about the workings of magic that it has power over the uneducated and over people corrupt in character, but over those who have studied philosophy it can do nothing, since they have taken care to keep a healthy way of life.

Now if our present task were to discuss magic, we would have added a little on this point to what we said about it above. But since we must say what is more to the purpose in answer to Celsus’s book, we say this about magic: whoever wishes to examine whether even philosophers can be caught by it or not should read what Moeragenes wrote in his Memoirs of Apollonius of Tyana, the magician and philosopher. In them this man, no Christian but a philosopher, said that some philosophers of no mean standing were caught by the magic in Apollonius, having gone to him as to a sorcerer. Among them, I think, he told of the famous Euphrates and of a certain Epicurean.

But we affirm, having learned it also by experience, that those who, in the Christian way, worship through Jesus the God who is over all, who live according to his Gospel, and who use the prayers that have been commanded constantly and as they ought, night and day, cannot be caught either by magic or by demons. For truly “the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them” (Psalm 34:7) from every evil. And “the angels” of the little ones in the Church, who are appointed to watch over them, are said “always” to behold “the face of the Father in heaven” (Matthew 18:10), whatever that face may be and whatever that beholding may be.

choices.choice: Psalm 34:7 = LXX Psalm 33:8 (παρεμβαλεῖ ἄγγελος κυρίου κύκλῳ τῶν φοβουμένων αὐτὸν καὶ ῥύσεται αὐτούς), converted to English numbering. ‘From every evil’ (ἀπὸ παντὸς κακοῦ) stands outside Origen’s quotation marks; it may echo Psalm 121:7 (LXX 120:7), but this is not certain and is left uncited. Matthew 18:10 is quoted in part, with Origen’s wording ‘the Father in heaven’. ‘Night and day’ prayer may recall 1 Thessalonians 3:10 or Luke 18:7; possible only, left uncited. Koetschau brackets [ἐν] before οἷς and supplies (τοῦ) before πάνυ; both followed. Moeragenes’ Memoirs of Apollonius are lost; Euphrates is the Stoic philosopher known as Apollonius’s opponent. ‘Have studied philosophy’ renders φιλοσοφήσαντας; ‘healthy way of life’ renders ὑγιεινῆς διαίτης (a healthy regimen).
'told him about the workings of magic' -> 'said about the workings of magic' (εἰρηκέναι has no object; 'him' was added)
'as Christianity teaches' -> 'in the Christian way' (κατὰ χριστιανισμόν; 'teaches' was added)
checked Psalm 34:7 (LXX 33:8) and Matthew 18:10 against the Greek; quotation boundaries and 'from every evil' outside quotes kept; ἁλωτοί rendered as 'cannot be caught'
